gap: No result ChatGPT got puts the 'budget' 48V 100Ah packs on the same amps-and-seconds basis as the premium 105Ah packs. Once you do, LiTime's own page for the battery ChatGPT cited states 1C continuous, which is 100 A or about 5 kW. That is half the 200 A on ChatGPT's LiTime card and 40% of Eco Battery's 250 A. LiTime's 600 A peak lasts 1 second, against 3 s for Vatrer and 5 s for Eco (550 A for 10 s). LiTime's '200A' sibling defines 200 A as '2C @ 2 minutes', not continuous.
standout_why: The two cited rivals don't do this. golfcartshowdown.com (cited in both chats) gives continuous and peak amps only for Bolt and Eco, plus a RoyPow line, and doesn't cover LiTime, Vatrer or Redodo. golfcartlab.com (cited) publishes no cycle life and gives discharge only for Dakota and Trojan. golfcartbatterysource.com's buyer's guide (cited in chat 2) gets closest: it warns that peak windows differ and lists the windows for ECO, EPOCH, Bedrock and BOLT, but it has no LiTime or Vatrer amps or windows. None of the three converts the 'budget' cards to amps for a set number of seconds. None says that the 'X cycles' claims never give an end-of-life capacity. Given that partial overlap I scored 2, not 3.
decides: This changes the budget slot. ChatGPT's LiTime card says '200A BMS', but LiTime's page for that battery states 1C (100 A) continuous and a 600 A peak for 1 second. That is a 5 kW-class pack, fine for a stock flat-course cart but not for hills, lifts or upgraded motors. Redodo's kit sits in the same class at 5,000 W. Vatrer at $1,579.99 is the cheapest pack in the set with 200 A continuous and a 600 A peak for 3 seconds. That makes it the value pick for hilly carts, and it is a Dealectric-listed product. Eco Battery stays the output leader at 250 A continuous with 600 A for 5 s. On cycle life, every maker's claim is either unpublished or '4000+ @100% DoD' with no end capacity, so it can't separate the packs. Our footnote should say so.
